Mar. 11, 2026) (precedential) (Dyk, J., joined by Prost, J., and Reyna, J.), reversing in part, vacating in part and remanding a judgment of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, No. 3:13-cv-00808-MHL (Lauck, C.J.)

item.title: Director adds American manufacturing and small-business status to the inter partes review institution decision
item.description:
Director John A. Squires told users of the Patent Trial and Appeal Board that, in deciding whether to institute inter partes review or post-grant review, he will consider three further factors: the extent to which products accused of infringement in a parallel proceeding are manufactured in the United States or tied to investment in American manufacturing; the extent to which the patent owner's own competing products, made, sold or licensed, are manufactured in the United States; and whether the petitioner is a small business that has been sued for infringement of the challenged patent. The memorandum rests on the direction in Sections 316(b) and 326(b) of Title 35 of the United States Code that the Director consider the effect of institution standards on the economy and the integrity of the patent system. It cites the movement of electronics and computing manufacturing overseas and notes that many frequent petitioners report no significant domestic manufacturing. Manufacturing includes where components are made and whether domestic products are finished abroad. For method claims, the relevant product is the device used to perform the method, such as the computer performing a method of operating a computer. Small-business status turns on Small Business Administration size standards, eligibility for reduced fees and other relevant facts. The factors apply to every proceeding whose discretionary brief is not yet due.
What it changes: Institution of an inter partes review now depends partly on the parties' factories, and for software and artificial intelligence patents the memorandum answers the threshold question of what the product is: for a method of operating a computer, it is the computer. A company sued on a software patent should establish, before discretionary briefing opens, where the servers, accelerators and devices that run the accused method are made and assembled, because that record now goes to the Director alongside the merits. A startup sued on a patent should identify itself as a small business in its petition with the evidence the memorandum names, since the third factor exists for petitioners in exactly that position. A patent owner whose technology is practiced by a domestic manufacturer, directly or under license, should put that fact in the record early. None of this changes the merits standard, but it changes what a defendant needs in hand in the first weeks after a complaint is served.
Memorandum, "Additional Discretionary Institution Considerations—U.S. Manufacturing and Small Business Use of AIA Proceedings" (Mar. 11, 2026), from John A. Squires, Under Secretary of Commerce for Intellectual Property and Director of the United States Patent and Trademark Office, to all PTAB users

item.title: Japan's Supreme Court refuses the DABUS appeal, leaving a natural person as the only possible inventor
item.description:
Japan's Supreme Court, Second Petty Bench, with Justice Kazumi Okamura presiding, decided on March 4, 2026 not to accept Stephen Thaler's appeal in the DABUS case, without giving reasons. Japanese Patent Application No. 2020-543051 entered the national phase from International Application PCT/IB2019/057809, which named the artificial intelligence system DABUS as inventor. When the applicant did not amend the national document to name a natural person, as Article 184-5 of the Patent Act requires, the Commissioner of the Japan Patent Office dismissed the application, and the Tokyo District Court upheld the dismissal on May 16, 2024. The Intellectual Property High Court affirmed on January 30, 2025. Reading the grant provision of Article 29(1) with the employee-invention provision of Article 35 and the requirements of Articles 36 and 66 that the inventor's name be stated and published, it held that the Patent Act "presupposes that the inventor is a natural person," so that no patent may be granted under the current statute for an invention made by artificial intelligence. It held that the inventor's name "is the mandatory information to be stated in a national document," that the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights imposes no obligation to protect such inventions, and that whether to grant them patents "is an issue that requires a discussion for legislation."
What it changes: Japan now stands with the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Australia, whose courts of last resort have each left in place or imposed a natural-person requirement for inventors, and the Japanese courts have said that any change belongs to the legislature. The practical point in Japan is procedural. The inventor's name is a required entry in the domestic document filed at national phase entry, a defective entry draws a correction order, and an applicant who will not name a human loses the application without examination. For a portfolio that enters Japan from international applications, confirm before the thirty-month national phase deadline that every inventor designation names the people who made the claimed invention, and settle any internal dispute about whether a model rather than an engineer produced a claimed feature before entry, not after a correction order arrives. The Supreme Court gave no reasons, so the High Court's judgment is the authority to cite.
Supreme Court of Japan, Second Petty Bench (Okamura, J., presiding), decision of March 4, 2026 declining to accept the appeal in the DABUS case, leaving in place Intellectual Property High Court (Second Division), judgment of January 30, 2025, 2024 (Gyo-Ko) 10006 (Shimizu, presiding), affirming Tokyo District Court, 2023 (Gyo-U) 5001 (May 16, 2024)

item.title: Supreme Court leaves in place the rule that a work generated by a machine alone has no author
item.description:
The Supreme Court denied Stephen Thaler's petition for a writ of certiorari, which asked whether works "outputted by" an artificial intelligence system "without a direct, traditional authorial contribution by a natural person can be copyrighted." The work was a two-dimensional image, "A Recent Entrance to Paradise," which Thaler's registration application attributed to his generative system, the Creativity Machine, and described as "[c]reated autonomously by machine." The Copyright Office refused registration because no human created the work, and the District of Columbia Circuit affirmed on March 18, 2025, holding that the Copyright Act requires a human author. The petition, filed October 9, 2025 with Ryan Abbott as counsel of record, also argued that Thaler owned the output as the system's owner and employer. The government waived a response, the Court requested one, and the Solicitor General's brief in opposition, filed January 23, 2026, argued that the case "does not implicate questions about the nature or extent of the human contribution" needed to register works made with artificial intelligence, because Thaler had disavowed any creative control, and that no court of appeals had reached his result. Amicus briefs were filed by Professors Shlomit Yanisky-Ravid, Lawrence Lessig and others and by Phyllis Schlafly Eagles. The petition was distributed for the conference of February 27, 2026 and denied on March 2, 2026.
What it changes: Human authorship is now as settled for copyright as the natural-person rule has been for inventorship since the Court declined the DABUS patent case in 2023, and the two regimes run in parallel: a machine can be neither author nor inventor, and the open question in both is how much a human must contribute. For a company whose code, documentation, designs or model outputs are increasingly generated by models, copyright will not protect the portions no human authored, so functionality worth protecting has to be claimed in a patent or held as a trade secret. Build one contribution record that serves both regimes: for each asset, which person framed the problem, chose and edited the outputs and made the decisions the claims or the registration rest on. The government's brief expressly set aside works made with the assistance of artificial intelligence, so registrations that disclose and disclaim machine-generated material remain available.
Thaler v. Perlmutter, No. 25-449 (U.S. Mar. 2, 2026) (petition for a writ of certiorari denied), leaving in place Thaler v. Perlmutter, No. 23-5233 (D.C. Cir. Mar. 18, 2025) (Millett, J., joined by Wilkins, J., and Rogers, S.J.), rehearing denied May 12, 2025

item.title: Applying a known machine learning technique to a new field is still abstract
item.description:
The patent claimed a method of processing natural language input using case-based reasoning, a machine learning technique that resolves ambiguity by drawing on stored historical examples in a metadata database. The Federal Circuit affirmed ineligibility, holding that generic use of artificial intelligence without other parameters is abstract, and that a conventional application of case-based reasoning, even to a novel environment, does not become eligible because the environment is new. The specification's own description of the database elements as well known in the art was used against the patentee at step two.
What it changes: Background sections that concede prior-art status get quoted back at step two. Describe what is conventional at the level of generality the claims do not depend on, and reserve the detailed description for the parts of the system that are actually new.
Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute v. Amazon.com, Inc., No. 24-1725 (Fed. Cir. Feb. 24, 2026) (Dyk, J.); U.S. Pat. No. 7,177,798

item.title: The UK Supreme Court drops Aerotel and moves the neural network patent fight to inventive step
item.description:
Emotional Perception's application claims a system that recommends media files using an artificial neural network trained on pairs of files compared by two measures, so that distances between file vectors track semantic distances. The Hearing Officer refused the application, the High Court allowed the applicant's appeal, and the Court of Appeal restored the refusal. The Supreme Court agreed that a network is "a set of instructions to manipulate data in a particular way" and so "a program for a computer" (para 87), however its weights were set. It held there is "a compelling case, in the light of G1/19, for rejecting the Aerotel approach" (para 64) and adopted the approach of the EPO Boards of Appeal. The claims involve technical means "because the ANN can only be implemented on some form of computer hardware" and refer to a database, a communications network and a user device (para 98), so their subject matter "constitutes an invention within the meaning of article 52" (para 100). Excluded matter is dealt with at inventive step through the intermediate step of G 1/19, under which "the sole criterion is whether the feature contributes to the technical character of the invention as a whole" (para 109). The court allowed the appeal, set aside the refusal and left inventive step to the Hearing Officer (para 118).
What it changes: The United Kingdom now examines computer-implemented and machine learning inventions the way the EPO does: any hardware clears the exclusion, and the contest moves to inventive step, where only features that contribute to technical character count. A trained network gets no special route, since the court held it is a program like any other. For United Kingdom filings and validations, draft as for the EPO: identify the technical effect each model feature produces, such as reduced computation, memory or latency or a measurement of a physical signal, state it in the specification, and tie it to the claimed features, because a recommendation that is merely more semantically apt is the kind of feature the intermediate step can filter out. Applications refused or narrowed under Aerotel deserve a fresh look, and pending appeals should be argued on the new approach. The court decided only the exclusion; the Hearing Officer still decides inventive step.
Emotional Perception AI Ltd v Comptroller-General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks [2026] UKSC 3 (11 February 2026) (Lord Briggs and Lord Leggatt, with whom Lord Hamblen, Lord Stephens and Lord Kitchin agree), allowing the appeal from [2024] EWCA Civ 825

item.title: China raises the inventiveness bar for artificial intelligence patents
item.description:
The amended guidelines state that changing only the application scenario or the target object of an existing artificial intelligence algorithm does not establish an inventive step. An applicant must show meaningful changes to model structure, parameters, training methods or technical effects. Disclosure requirements were tightened at the same time: a specification must describe the model architecture including modules, layers and connections, the training steps and key parameters, and the technical relationship between the input and the output data. Examiners may examine the description alongside the claims. The guidelines also permit rejection on public policy grounds where an invention involves unlawful collection or use of personal data, or algorithmic decision-making on discriminatory criteria.
What it changes: China has arrived at the Federal Circuit's central point from the opposite direction. Applying a known model to a new field is not enough in either country. For a family filed in the United States, Europe and China, the model architecture and the training description have to sit in the priority document, because none of the three offices will let that material be added afterwards.
Amended Patent Examination Guidelines, China National Intellectual Property Administration Order No. 84, issued 10 November 2025, effective 1 January 2026

item.title: The examination manual now lists improving how a machine learning model trains as an improvement to technology
item.description:
The United States Patent and Trademark Office revised Sections 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a) and 2106.05(f) of the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure to incorporate Ex parte Desjardins, the Appeals Review Panel decision of September 26, 2025 designated precedential on November 4, 2025. Section 2106.05(a) adds two examples of technological improvements: "An improved way of training a machine learning model that protected the model's knowledge about previous tasks" and "Improvements to computer component or system performance based upon adjustments to parameters of a machine learning model." Section 2106.04(d) now summarizes Desjardins, where a claim to training a model on a series of tasks recited a mathematical concept but integrated it into a practical application because the specification described improvements to how the model operates, including overcoming catastrophic forgetting. Examiners are told not to evaluate claims "at such a high level of generality" that technical limitations are dismissed, nor to dismiss elements as generic computer components without considering whether they provide an improvement, and that "the claim must include the components or steps of the invention that provide the improvement described in the specification," though it need not recite the improvement. The Director's December 4 memorandum on Subject Matter Eligibility Declarations requires examiners to weigh on its merits an optional declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 offering expert testimony or objective data on a technological improvement.
What it changes: Every response to an eligibility rejection of a machine learning claim under Section 101 of Title 35 of the United States Code should now cite Section 2106.05(a) examples xiii and xiv and the Desjardins paragraph in Section 2106.04(d), because the manual binds the examiner in a way an argument from a single Appeals Review Panel decision did not. The drafting rule is stated in the manual's own words: the specification has to describe the improvement to how the model trains or runs, and the claim has to contain the steps that produce it. That is the line between Desjardins and Recentive Analytics v. Fox, where applying a generic model to a new data environment was abstract. The declaration route rewards keeping evidence in the invention record, such as ablation results, memory and latency measurements and benchmark comparisons, because a declaration can prove an improvement the specification describes but cannot add one it omits. The manual governs examiners only; courts apply Recentive.
Memorandum, "Advance notice of change to the MPEP in light of Ex Parte Desjardins" (Dec. 5, 2025), from Charles Kim, Deputy Commissioner for Patents, to the Patent Examining Corps; Memorandum, "Subject Matter Eligibility Declarations" (Dec. 4, 2025), from John A. Squires, Under Secretary of Commerce for Intellectual Property and Director of the United States Patent and Trademark Office, to the Patent Examining Corps

item.title: USPTO rescinds the 2024 inventorship guidance and treats artificial intelligence as a tool only
item.description:
The USPTO withdrew its February 2024 guidance on artificial-intelligence-assisted inventions and replaced it with guidance treating artificial intelligence systems as tools rather than as candidate joint inventors. The Office stated that the Pannu joint-inventorship factors apply only among natural persons and cannot be extended to an artificial intelligence system, and directed examiners to apply the ordinary inventorship standard without a separate pathway for applications involving artificial intelligence.
What it changes: Thaler v. Vidal still controls: every named inventor must be a natural person. The practical change is that inventorship questionnaires no longer need a separate significant-contribution analysis for the model itself; they need a record of which human made the conception decisions the claims rest on.
Revised Inventorship Guidance for AI-Assisted Inventions, 90 Fed. Reg. 54636 (Nov. 28, 2025), rescinding 89 Fed. Reg. 10043 (Feb. 13, 2024)

item.title: An English court holds that Stable Diffusion's weights are not an infringing copy of the images used to train it
item.description:
Getty Images sued Stability AI in the High Court over the Stable Diffusion image models. By the end of trial Getty had abandoned its primary copyright claim over training, there being no evidence of training in the United Kingdom, its claim over outputs, because prompt blocking had achieved the relief sought, and its database right claim. What remained was secondary infringement under sections 22 and 23 of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, on the theory that the model is an "infringing copy" because making its weights would have infringed if done in the United Kingdom, trade mark claims under section 10 of the Trade Marks Act 1994 over Getty and iStock watermarks in outputs, and passing off. The judgment records that the model does not store training data. Mrs Justice Joanna Smith held that an "article" can be intangible, but that an infringing copy must at some time have contained or stored a copy of the work, and because Getty accepted, as both sides' experts agreed, that the weights contain no copies of its works, the secondary infringement claim failed. The trade mark claims succeeded only for a few watermarked outputs of the first two model versions, findings described as extremely limited; the claims for the SD XL and v1.6 models and under section 10(3) failed, and passing off added nothing.
What it changes: The judgment accepts, on agreed expert evidence, that trained weights do not contain the works they were trained on, and it treats the model as the developer's own technical object rather than a copy of anyone's images. That supports protecting weights as a trade secret and claiming the training method and model structure as inventions in their own right. The case was decided on expert evidence of what the parameters represent, and a patent specification should carry the same kind of explanation, because what the weights encode is also what written description and sufficiency will be measured against. The territorial point cuts across patents too: Getty abandoned the training claim for want of evidence of training in the United Kingdom, and a training-method claim is likewise infringed only where training is done, so portfolios need claims to the trained model, the inference system and its uses in the markets where the model is deployed. This is a first-instance judgment on a narrowed case.
Getty Images (US) Inc v Stability AI Ltd [2025] EWHC 2863 (Ch) (4 November 2025) (Joanna Smith J), Case No. IL-2023-000007

item.title: The USPTO Director takes over inter partes review institution and proposes barring review where a court trial will come first
item.description:
Director John Squires announced that from October 20, 2025 the Director will determine whether to institute inter partes review and post-grant review, in consultation with at least three judges of the Patent Trial and Appeal Board. Where institution is appropriate on at least one ground for one challenged claim, the Director issues a summary notice granting institution; otherwise a summary notice denying it. Routine institution decisions are limited to summary notices, the Director may write a decision on novel or important factual or legal issues, and may refer a petition to Board members for detailed treatment such as complex claim construction, priority or real party in interest questions. Instituted trials go to three-judge panels, which no longer decide institution on the merits; briefing under the March 26, 2025 interim procedures continues. The same day the United States Patent and Trademark Office published proposed rules that would bar institution unless each petitioner stipulates that it and its privies will not pursue invalidity under Section 102 or 103 of Title 35 of the United States Code in any other forum; bar it where a challenged claim was previously upheld by a district court, the International Trade Commission or a Board final written decision; and bar it where a district court trial or Commission determination on those grounds will more likely than not come before the final written decision.
What it changes: For a company defending against software or artificial intelligence patents, the Board is now a forum the Director opens case by case, usually without explanation, and the invalidity case should be budgeted and built for district court from the start, with the petition as an option rather than the plan. If the proposed rules are adopted as written, an instituted petition would cost the petitioner its anticipation and obviousness defenses everywhere else, so the choice of forum for the best prior art would have to be made once, early, and with the trial team in the room. Defendants sued in fast districts would rarely qualify at all. Patent owners holding older software and machine learning patents gain bargaining power in licensing and should assert where trial dates come quickly. The memorandum is in effect; the rules are proposed and may change before adoption.
Memorandum, "Director Institution of AIA Trial Proceedings" (Oct. 17, 2025), from John A. Squires, Under Secretary of Commerce for Intellectual Property and Director of the United States Patent and Trademark Office, to all Patent Trial and Appeal Board judges; Revision to Rules of Practice before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, 90 Fed. Reg. 48335 (Oct. 17, 2025) (proposed rule)

item.title: Appeals Review Panel finds machine learning claims eligible on efficiency-based technical improvements
item.description:
The USPTO Director convened an Appeals Review Panel to review a Board rejection of machine learning method claims under § 101. The panel disagreed with the Board's step-two analysis and held that technological advantages of the claimed method, including reduced storage requirements and efficiency gains, amount to a practical application of the abstract idea where those advantages are reflected in the claim language itself.
What it changes: This is the single most useful citation available in prosecution right now for a machine learning claim carrying a resource-efficiency benefit. It works only if the efficiency is recited in the claim, not merely asserted in the specification or the response.
Ex parte Desjardins, Appeals Review Panel decision (Sept. 26, 2025) (convened sua sponte by the Director)

item.title: A federal court preliminarily approves Anthropic's $1.5 billion settlement over pirated training books, about $3,000 a work
item.description:
After Judge William Alsup's June 23, 2025 order held that training on books was fair use but that pirated library copies were not, the court on July 17, 2025 certified a "LibGen & PiLiMi Pirated Books Class," and trial was set for December 1, 2025. On September 5 the class moved for preliminary approval of a settlement. Anthropic will pay at least $1.5 billion plus interest into a non-reversionary fund; with around 500,000 works in the class, class counsel estimated a gross recovery of $3,000 per work, and Anthropic will pay a further $3,000 for each work added above 500,000. Anthropic will destroy the original files it obtained from Library Genesis and the Pirate Library Mirror and copies originating from them, subject to preservation obligations. The release covers only past conduct through August 25, 2025, and releases no claim, past or future, arising from allegedly infringing outputs of Anthropic's models. Class counsel called it the largest publicly reported copyright recovery and compared the per-work figure with the $750 statutory minimum and the $200 floor for innocent infringement. Funds are allocated equally per work. On September 25, after a September 8 hearing and written questions from the court, Judge Alsup granted preliminary approval of the class settlement, the plan of distribution and the plan for notice.
What it changes: Pirated training data now has a price per work, and a model budget that does not carry acquisition or licensing cost for its corpus is missing a line. For the patent program the consequence is in diligence and continuity. A patent on a model, a training method or a product built on the model does nothing to offset liability for the corpus the model learned from, so any acquisition of a company, a portfolio or a model license should ask for the acquisition record of the training data alongside the patent schedule. The destruction term shows that a settlement can take datasets out of service, and a product line whose patented features depend on a model trained on those datasets needs a retraining plan. Output claims were expressly left open, so the filtering and attribution mechanisms that keep a model from reproducing its training text remain worth both engineering investment and patent filings.
Bartz v. Anthropic PBC, No. 3:24-cv-05417-WHA (N.D. Cal. Sept. 25, 2025) (Alsup, J.) (minute entry granting preliminary approval of class settlement, Dkt. 427), on the Motion for Preliminary Approval of Class Settlement (Dkt. 363, filed Sept. 5, 2025)

item.title: xAI sues OpenAI over engineers who left with training code, inference code and data center know-how
item.description:
xAI sued three OpenAI entities for misappropriation under the Defend Trade Secrets Act, intentional interference with prospective economic advantage, and unfair competition under California law. The complaint alleges that the same OpenAI recruiter pursued two early xAI engineers. Xuechen Li, who worked on training Grok, allegedly uploaded the entire xAI code base to a personal cloud account on July 25, 2025, reportedly admitted taking it with a slide deck on training and tuning methods, and in xAI's earlier suit against him was restrained on September 2 from any role at OpenAI until the material was deleted. Jimmy Fraiture, who led the production inference team, allegedly transferred source code by AirDrop on July 31, including inference cluster code, training and infrastructure code written by others, and co-founders' experimental folders. A senior finance executive allegedly took knowledge of xAI's data center deployment. The complaint pleads that "Trade secrets protect nearly all of xAI's developments—model weights, training data, tuning methods, know-how, and more," and lists its measures: security training, background checks, the NIST 800-171 Rev. 3 baseline, SOC 2 Type II compliance, full disk encryption, a written security policy, confidentiality and invention assignment agreements, and termination certifications. It seeks damages, injunctive relief, removal of xAI information from OpenAI's systems, and destruction of OpenAI technology or models developed with it. These are allegations, not findings.
What it changes: The complaint reads as a checklist for any model developer that relies on trade secrets: name the secret, show who had access, show the measures, and prove the taking, here from forensic logs, cloud records and admissions. A company that cannot produce each of those for its training code, inference stack and infrastructure methods has a weaker claim than it thinks. The remedy requested, destruction of models built with the information, also shows what a recipient risks when it hires a competitor's engineers. For the patent decision, the techniques most likely to leave with an engineer, how inference clusters stay reliable, how training infrastructure is built, how data centers come up fast, are the ones where a patent pays, because it is enforced against a competitor without proving anyone took anything. Hiring from a competitor also calls for screening the new hire's invention disclosures for inventorship and derivation problems before they become applications.
X.AI Corp. and X.AI LLC v. OpenAI, Inc., OpenAI Global, LLC and OpenAI OpCo, LLC, No. 3:25-cv-08133 (N.D. Cal. filed Sept. 24, 2025) (complaint); see X.AI Corp. v. Li, No. 3:25-cv-07292 (N.D. Cal. filed Aug. 28, 2025)

item.title: A claim reciting a motor that physically moves a dumbbell's weight selector is a machine, not an abstract idea
item.description:
United States Patent No. 7,578,771 claims a weight selection and adjustment system. Claim 1 recites a selectorized dumbbell with nested left and right stacks of weight plates, a handle, and a movable selector whose adjustment positions couple selected numbers of plates to each end, together with an electric motor "operatively connected to the selector" that "physically moves the selector into the adjustment position corresponding to the desired exercise weight." Claim 20 adds a data entry device through which the user inputs a weight selection that controls the motor. Judge Jill Parrish of the District of Utah dismissed claims 1 through 18 and 20 under Rule 12(b)(6) as directed to the abstract idea of automated weight stacking under Section 101 of Title 35 of the United States Code. The Federal Circuit reversed at step one. Claim 1 is "limited to a specific implementation of a technological improvement" to selectorized dumbbells and is "directed to an eligible mechanical invention," unlike the "do it on a computer" claims in University of Florida Research Foundation v. General Electric and the Chamberlain v. Techtronic claims, which did not recite the barrier they controlled. Citing Diamond v. Diehr, the panel declined to ignore limitations found in the prior art, and it cautioned against conflating novelty and obviousness with step one. Claims 2 through 18 and 20, not argued separately, stood with claim 1.
What it changes: Machine learning in a physical product, in robotics, vehicles, medical devices or industrial control, is claimable at step one when the claim recites the machine the model acts on and the actuator that does the acting. A claim that says a controller issues a command based on a model's output, without the structure that receives it, reads like Chamberlain; a claim that names the mechanism, its coupling and the physical movement reads like this one. Draft the independent claim to include the plant, the actuator, the coupling and the physical result, and put the model's role in the step that selects the movement. In prosecution and litigation, Diehr is now applied in a precedential opinion against the argument that conventional components can be stripped out before asking what a claim is directed to, and that argument belongs under novelty and obviousness. The panel noted that this was a simple mechanical invention, decided on a motion to dismiss.
PowerBlock Holdings, Inc. v. iFit, Inc., No. 2024-1177 (Fed. Cir. Aug. 11, 2025) (precedential) (Stoll, J., joined by Taranto, J., and Scarsi, District Judge, sitting by designation), reversing PowerBlock Holdings, Inc. v. iFit, Inc., No. 1:22-cv-00132-JNP-CMR (D. Utah Sept. 29, 2023) (Parrish, J.)

item.title: Director's memorandum narrows the mental-process rejection and imposes an evidence standard
item.description:
The Director issued a memorandum to the software and business-method art units reminding examiners that a process falls in the mental-process grouping only if a human could practically perform it, not merely if a human could theoretically perform some version of it, and that an eligibility rejection must be supported under the same preponderance-of-the-evidence standard as any other rejection.
What it changes: Cite the memorandum by name in the response and make the examiner carry the evidentiary burden. Where a claim recites a computation no person could practically perform — the data volume, the latency requirement, or the model size makes it impossible — say so on the record with the numbers from the specification.
Memorandum, “Reminders on Evaluating Subject Matter Eligibility of Claims under 35 U.S.C. 101” (Aug. 4, 2025), directed to Technology Centers 2100, 2600, and 3600

item.title: General-purpose model providers in the European Union must now publish a summary of their training content
item.description:
Chapter V of the Artificial Intelligence Act, on general-purpose models, applies from 2 August 2025 under Article 113(b), with the exception of Article 101 on fines. Article 53(1) requires every provider of a general-purpose model to keep technical documentation "including its training and testing process"; to give information and documentation to providers that integrate the model, "[w]ithout prejudice to the need to observe and protect intellectual property rights and confidential business information"; to "put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights," including reservations of rights under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790; and to "draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training" on a template from the AI Office. Models released under a free and open-source licence are exempt from the first two duties only, and not if they carry systemic risk. Under Article 111(3), providers whose models were placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027. The Commission published the voluntary General-Purpose AI Code of Practice on 10 July 2025, with chapters on transparency, including a model documentation form, copyright, and safety and security, and on 24 July 2025 adopted the mandatory template, under which the summary lists the main data collections and explains other sources.
What it changes: The training content summary is a mandatory publication for every general-purpose model placed on the European Union market, and anything it discloses about data selection, filtering, deduplication, synthetic data generation or handling of opt-outs is prior art from the day it is posted and no longer a trade secret. Patent counsel should see each summary before it is published. Any pipeline invention the summary would reveal should be filed first, and the summary should be written at the level of generality the template requires and no lower. The technical documentation and downstream information duties do not publish anything, but documentation handed to integrating providers travels under contract, so the confidentiality terms in those agreements need the same review as a license. For models already on the market the 2027 deadline leaves time to file on pipeline inventions that the first summary would expose.
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Articles 53, 111(3) and 113(b), obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models applicable from 2 August 2025; European Commission, General-Purpose AI Code of Practice (10 July 2025); European Commission, Explanatory Notice and Template for the Public Summary of Training Content for general-purpose AI models (24 July 2025)

item.title: The White House artificial intelligence plan says nothing about patents and pushes open weights and full-stack exports
item.description:
The White House released a plan organized in three pillars, accelerating innovation, building infrastructure, and leading in international diplomacy and security, each with recommended policy actions for federal agencies, and the President signed three executive orders the same day. The plan does not use the words patent, copyright or fair use, and does not mention the United States Patent and Trademark Office. Intellectual property appears once, in a section titled "Protect Commercial and Government AI Innovations," which states that the government must address security risks to American companies, "talent, intellectual property, and systems," and recommends that the Department of Defense, the Department of Homeland Security, the Center for AI Standards and Innovation and the intelligence community work with leading developers to defend their innovations against threats including malicious cyber actors and insiders. A section titled "Encourage Open-Source and Open-Weight AI" describes such models as "made freely available by developers for anyone in the world to download and modify" and recommends actions to expand access to computing for startups and academics and to drive adoption of open models by small and medium-sized businesses. The export order directs the Secretary of Commerce, within 90 days, to establish an American exports program and to call for proposals from industry-led consortia for full-stack packages combining chips and servers, "data pipelines and labeling systems," models, security measures and applications for specific uses.
What it changes: Federal policy will not settle eligibility, inventorship or the copyright status of training data; those questions stay with the courts, the Office and Congress, and patent budgets should assume no relief from this plan. Two parts of the plan still change patent decisions. The push for open-weight models matters because a released model, its weights and its technical report are published prior art everywhere on the day of release, so any company answering that call should decide which architecture, training and serving inventions to file on before release rather than after. The export program will put American model and infrastructure packages into allied markets selected by Commerce, and foreign filing budgets for model, data pipeline and data center inventions should follow the markets those consortia enter. The plan's language on insider threats fits a trade secret program and offers no substitute for one.
The White House, "Winning the Race: America's AI Action Plan" (July 23, 2025), issued with Executive Orders "Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government," "Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure" and "Promoting the Export of the American AI Technology Stack" (July 23, 2025)

item.title: A product on the market is prior art at the EPO even if no one could analyse or reproduce it
item.description:
The referral came from Technical Board 3.3.03 in an opposition appeal against Mitsui Chemicals' European patent No. 2 626 911, where the closest prior art was a commercial polymer, ENGAGE 8400. Opinion G 1/92 had been read to make a marketed product state of the art only if the skilled person could analyse and reproduce it, and the referring board asked whether a product that could not be analysed and reproduced without undue burden is excluded, and whether published information about it still counts. The Enlarged Board answered that a product put on the market before the filing date "cannot be excluded from the state of the art within the meaning of Article 54(2) EPC for the sole reason that its composition or internal structure could not be analysed and reproduced by the skilled person before that date," and that technical information about such a product made public before filing is state of the art "irrespective of whether the skilled person could analyse and reproduce the product." It held that the answer in G 1/92 "cannot be maintained in its entirety," that "all analysable properties of the product put on the market will belong to the state of the art," that a non-reproducible product "still cannot be ignored for novelty," and that its features may, but need not, enter the inventive step analysis.
What it changes: A model that ships is prior art at the EPO for everything the public can observe or analyse about it, even though nobody outside the company can rebuild its weights or its training run. That reaches the behaviour of a deployed model, its outputs and interface, its published model card and technical report, and, for a model distributed on a device, whatever architecture and parameters a skilled person can extract from the file. Europe has no general grace period, so a company that launches first and files afterwards on what its product does will meet its own product as novelty-destroying or obviousness art. File before any public beta, application programming interface access or on-device release, and treat benchmark disclosures and model documentation as publications on the filing calendar. For freedom-to-operate work, a competitor's earlier product is now usable art even where its internals were secret.
Decision of the Enlarged Board of Appeal G 1/23 (2 July 2025), Solar cell sealing material, and solar cell module / Mitsui Chemicals, on referral from Technical Board of Appeal decision T 438/19

item.title: Two federal judges find training on books fair use on their records, and leave pirated libraries and market dilution open
item.description:
Judge William Alsup granted Anthropic summary judgment that using books to train the large language models behind Claude was fair use under Section 107 of Title 17 of the United States Code, calling the training use "exceedingly transformative," and held that scanning purchased print books into digital library copies was fair use as well. He denied summary judgment for the more than seven million pirated copies Anthropic downloaded from Books3, Library Genesis and the Pirate Library Mirror for a permanent central library, holding that "Anthropic had no entitlement to use pirated copies for its central library," and set those copies for trial. The order noted that the authors alleged no infringing outputs and that the Claude service placed software between users and the model to block them. On June 25 Judge Vince Chhabria granted Meta summary judgment on fair use for training Llama on thirteen authors' books taken from shadow libraries, finding the use highly transformative, Llama "not capable of generating enough text from the plaintiffs' books to matter," and the authors not entitled to a market for licensing their works as training data. He called market dilution the potentially winning argument, found no evidence of it, and stated that the ruling "does not stand for the proposition that Meta's use of copyrighted materials to train its language models is lawful."
What it changes: Both judges treated training as transformative. Judge Alsup then separated the training copies from the pirated library and sent the library to trial, and Judge Chhabria ruled on the absence of market evidence, so the records that decide these cases are how the copies were obtained and kept and what the model can reproduce. The acquisition record also feeds the patent program. A specification that names its training corpus is a public admission about where the data came from, so describe training data by its properties and processing and keep sources in the confidential provenance file. Keep that file per training run, with source, license, acquisition method and retention. The output filter that mattered in Bartz is engineering worth an invention disclosure, since blocking regurgitation is now both a technical feature and a litigation defense. These are district court rulings on particular records, and the Meta decision binds only its thirteen plaintiffs.
Bartz v. Anthropic PBC, No. C 24-05417 WHA (N.D. Cal. June 23, 2025) (Alsup, J.) (order on fair use); Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 23-cv-03417-VC (N.D. Cal. June 25, 2025) (Chhabria, J.) (order denying the plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment and granting Meta's cross-motion for partial summary judgment)

item.title: A patent in force almost eight years carries settled expectations that can defeat an inter partes review petition
item.description:
Acting Director Coke Morgan Stewart denied a petition for inter partes review of United States Patent No. 9,771,169, AXA Power's patent on a preconditioned air unit for parked aircraft, which issued in September 2017. The decision applies the interim process announced in her memorandum of March 26, 2025, under which the Director, consulting at least three judges of the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, decides discretionary denial on briefs from both sides. One listed factor is the "settled expectations of the parties, such as the length of time the claims have been in force." The Acting Director found that "the challenged patent has been in force almost eight years, creating settled expectations." She stated that "there is no bright-line rule on when expectations become settled," that expectations grow more settled the longer a patent is in force, and compared the six-year limit on recovering damages in Section 286 of Title 35 of the United States Code. Because issued patents and published applications are public, "actual notice of a patent or of possible infringement is not necessary to create settled expectations." The petitioner did "not provide any persuasive reasoning" why review was a proper use of the resources of the United States Patent and Trademark Office. The decision rejected the patent owner's Section 325(d) arguments and denied institution under Section 314(a).
What it changes: The age of the patent is now an argument against review, and the clock runs from issuance rather than from the day the patent is asserted. A company shipping artificial intelligence or software products that faces a software patent issued six or more years ago should assume the Board may decline to hear its invalidity case and should build that case, art and expert together, for district court from the first week of the dispute. Competitor patent watching becomes a timing question: a patent that matters to the roadmap should be challenged while it is young, before settled expectations accrue, rather than held in reserve until assertion. For patent owners the calculus runs the other way. An older parent patent is now harder to attack at the Office than a newly issued continuation, so assertion campaigns should lead with the oldest claims that read on the product. The decision is a single interim-process ruling, and it disclaims any bright line.
Dabico Airport Solutions Inc. v. AXA Power ApS, IPR2025-00408, Paper 21 (June 18, 2025) (Coke Morgan Stewart, Acting Under Secretary of Commerce for Intellectual Property and Acting Director of the United States Patent and Trademark Office), granting the patent owner's request for discretionary denial of institution of review of United States Patent No. 9,771,169 B2
